title: What are false positives?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain false positives and false negatives in medical testing, using Bayesian-style examples of how accurate tests can still produce many false positives. They cover the costs and emotional toll of follow-up testing, the Annals of Family Medicine and Cancer Epidemiology Biomarkers studies, and the Choosing Wisely campaign. Discussion moves to Pap smear and mammogram overdiagnosis, colonoscopy versus stool-based colorectal cancer screening, and drug tests, where false positives come from prescription and OTC drugs, poppy seeds, quinine in tonic water, and cocaine on dollar bills. The episode closes with HIV ELISA testing accuracy and a listener email from teacher Mr. Swedman about types of reproductive isolation.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about hosting alone and tease the episode on false positives, promising a controversy angle.

segments.title: True and false positives and negatives
segments.summary: The hosts define the four possible medical test results: true positive, true negative, false positive, and false negative. They explain that a test's accuracy does not mean a positive result has a 99 percent chance of being correct.

segments.title: Bayesian reasoning and follow-up testing
segments.summary: Using a 10,000-person example with a 99 percent accurate test, they show that roughly half of positive results can be false positives. They then discuss how follow-up tests can cost money, take time, and cause stress.

segments.title: Emotional and financial costs of false positives
segments.summary: They cite the Annals of Family Medicine study on false positives across repeated cancer screenings, and a 2008 study finding that follow-up care after false positives cost about a thousand dollars for women and about eleven hundred for men.

segments.title: Choosing Wisely and wasteful healthcare
segments.summary: They describe the National Academy of Sciences finding that about thirty percent of US healthcare spending was wasteful, and the Choosing Wisely campaign from the American Board of Internal Medicine and Consumer Reports.

segments.title: Pap smears and mammograms
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Pap smear's false positive rate and cervical cancer deaths. They then cover mammogram false positives, the radiologist's role, the biopsy follow-ups, and the changing screening age recommendations from the American Cancer Society.

segments.title: Colorectal cancer screening: colonoscopy and stool tests
segments.summary: They explain that colorectal cancer is the second leading cancer death in the US and that many people avoid colonoscopies. They describe the procedure and mention stool-based alternatives like colon Guard, which have high false positive rates.

segments.title: Drug test false positives
segments.summary: They explain that prescription and over-the-counter medicines can cause false positive drug tests, and that an estimated seven to fifteen million people a year get one. They note secondhand smoke is not a cause of a marijuana false positive.

segments.title: Surprising sources of false drug test results
segments.summary: They cover cocaine traces on dollar bills per an NYU study, poppy seeds and opium residue (Seinfeld reference), ibuprofen, barbiturates, Benzedrine, Kerouac, Sudafed, and quinine in tonic water mimicking heroin.

segments.title: HIV ELISA testing accuracy
segments.summary: The hosts describe the multi-step HIV testing process using ELISA screens with a confirmatory test, which yields a false positive rate of about one in 250,000 tests in the US.

segments.title: Listener mail: types of reproductive isolation
segments.summary: A listener email from teacher Mr. Swedman describes types of reproductive isolation: geographic, ecological, behavioral, temporal, gametic, and mechanical.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and email contact details and sign off.
